subject: history_social
passage: Accounts of the Ming dynasty's naval expeditions of the early 1400s, led by the admiral Zheng He, credit the largest "treasure ships" with lengths of roughly 120 meters, which would make them several times longer than the ships Columbus sailed decades later. Some historians accept the figure, noting that an enormous rudder post was excavated at the site of a former Ming shipyard. Others point out that the dimensions come from texts written long after the voyages and that wooden hulls of that length would have been extraordinarily difficult to keep from bending and leaking. What both sides agree on is that the fleets were vast overall, with dozens of ships and many thousands of crew members.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Historians dispute the size of Zheng He's largest ships but agree that his fleets were vast.
choices.B: A huge excavated rudder post has proved that Zheng He's largest ships were about 120 meters long.
choices.C: Wooden ships cannot be built longer than about 120 meters without bending and leaking.
choices.D: Some historians doubt reports of the ships' length because the reports were written much later.

explanation.why: The text presents a reported figure, then two camps: some historians accept it (citing the rudder post), and others doubt it (late sources, structural problems). The final sentence adds what "both sides agree on": the fleets were vast. A main idea must cover both the disagreement and the agreement.
explanation.A: Correct. This covers the whole text: the dispute over the largest ships' size and the shared view that the fleets were enormous.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The rudder post is evidence one side cites, not proof; the text presents the length as disputed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says such hulls would have been "extraordinarily difficult" to keep sound, not impossible, and it makes no general claim about all wooden ships.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This gives only one side's argument and leaves out both the opposing view and the point of agreement.
